question: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

A report1 on air quality around 34 schools in Logroño, Spain, concludes that 97 % of the schools tested exceed the WHO recommendations for NO₂, while more than 45 % exceed the new limits for 2030 set by Directive (EU) 2024/2881. The study highlights a close link between the intensity of motorised traffic and the levels of pollution recorded around schools. These findings come against the backdrop of recent decisions to reduce sustainable mobility infrastructure in the city and remove cycle lanes, even though the Commission has highlighted the role active mobility has to play in improving urban air quality. 1.
What is the Commission’s view of the results of this study, taking the new European objectives on air quality and the protection of children’s health into account?
In the Commission’s view, is removing active and sustainable mobility infrastructure in urban environments that have problems with air pollution compatible with these objectives?

What measures will the Commission take to foster healthy environments for schools and to support local authorities that focus on reducing motorised traffic, increasing active mobility and improving air quality?
https://www.ecologistasenaccion.org/365706/.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission takes note of the referenced study aimed to serve the Spanish authorities in their implementation of the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive1. Given the division of responsibilities under the Directive, it is up to the Member States’ authorities to decide on the relevance of different inputs, in their decision-making process. The Directive introduces stricter EU air quality standards, including for nitrogen dioxide (NO2), to be attained by 2030. Where from 2026 until 2029 the levels of air pollutants are higher than air quality standards, authorities need to adopt roadmaps establishing measures to reach these. The Directive also improves the rules on air quality monitoring, requiring authorities to consider, to the extent possible, sensitive population and vulnerable groups – such as children – when deciding where to measure at hotspot locations. While the Directive establishes an indicative list of measures to be considered2, including measures to encourage a modal shift towards active mobility and less polluting forms of transport, the final choice of measures is up to the Member States. Active mobility infrastructure plays an important role, in urban areas, in line also with the New EU Urban Mobility Framework3 and the European Declaration on Cycling4. In addition, the Commission highlights relevant EU urban initiatives that provide targeted support to local authorities, notably the European Mobility Week5 and the Green City Accord6.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/2881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on ambient air

quality and cleaner air for Europe (recast), OJ L, 2024/2881, 20.11.2024. 2 Annex VIII of Directive (EU) 2024/2881. 3 COM(2021) 811 final; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52021DC0811. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202402377. 5 https://mobilityweek.eu. 6 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/urban-environment/green-city-accord_en.
